Many ChaaS marketing materials prominently feature the function of managing the life cycle of an EV charging system, often using terms like “turnkey solution.” The system life cycle spans across design, procurement, construction, operation, maintenance and support, and end-of-life. Because it encompasses the lifetime of the system, life cycle management functions overlap with other (economic, technical, societal) functions. For example, ChaaS management of design and construction (what we categorize as a managerial function) should result in an expertly designed system (a technical function). As a “managerial” function, however, the emphasis is that the ChaaS provider manages and coordinates tasks that would otherwise be left to the user, and which the user may not be willing or able to do. For many, the capacity to host EVSE may be incumbent on the ability to offload life cycle management responsibilities such as planning, repair, replacement, and disposal, which is a lesson the industry has learned by experience.44 Societal functions ChaaS can function for societal benefit, including by helping to accelerate the adoption of EVs, addressing equity challenges in electric transportation, and reducing the carbon emissions impact of transportation. Policy incentives or mandates to support these societal aims are in place or are being considered and would enable such societal benefits to be internalized to the ChaaS business model. Electrification of transportation offers the potential to reduce the environmental impact of the transportation sector, which would benefit human health and mitigate emissions driving climate change [72]. ChaaS can help to accelerate the electrification of transportation via each of the categories of functions previously described (economic, technical, and managerial). Unfavorable economics, including unacceptably high infrastructure costs and unacceptable levels of risk, have been cited as key reasons for the decision not to adopt EVs [37]. This is true across sectors, including the “difficult-to-electrify” sectors such as long-haul freight [73]. There may be applications for which the economic benefits of ChaaS are sufficient to make EV adoption feasible where it would otherwise not be. Non-economic factors also serve as barriers to adoption, including burdensome EVSE procurement processes and lack of access to charging infrastructure. ChaaS has the potential to address each of these barriers.
